product.title: Gantry
product.description: A game-agnostic content framework. Experiences compose into a declared dependency tree and activate in observable stages, with game feature plugins reference counted across swaps, so shipped content and side-loaded mods travel the same path with load order computed instead of curated. Loads are tracked as named, tagged scopes, so a loading bar can say "Environment 12/40" and a live editor panel can attribute a hitch to the scope that caused it.

types.summary: Outcome of checking a shipped unit against the running build.

values.name: Compatible
values.doc: Safe to mount and activate.

values.name: EngineMismatch
values.doc: Built against a different engine. Code in the unit is binary incompatible; never negotiable.

values.name: GameVersionOutOfRange
values.doc: Engine matches, but the game build is outside the range the unit declares it supports.

values.name: Unstamped
values.doc: Never stamped. Almost always an uncooked asset being asked a cooked-build question.

types.summary: Whether an experience can be played right now, and if not, why not.

values.name: Available
values.doc: Present, compatible, chain fully resolvable. Playable.

values.name: NotInstalled
values.doc: Listed by an installed ancestor but its own content is not mounted. Offer as a download.

values.name: Incompatible
values.doc: Present, but built for a different engine or game version.

values.name: MissingDependency
values.doc: Present, but a required parent is absent. Visible orphan; cannot activate.

types.summary: Where an experience is in its lifecycle.

values.name: None
values.doc: Nothing set.

values.name: Resolving
values.doc: Definition is being resolved and loaded.

values.name: Loading
values.doc: Stages are running.

values.name: Ready
values.doc: Every stage completed; the experience is live.

values.name: Deactivating
values.doc: Stages are being torn down.

values.name: Failed
values.doc: A stage failed. The experience is not usable.

types.summary: Lifecycle of a load scope.

values.name: Pending
values.doc: Opened, nothing attached yet.

values.name: Loading
values.doc: At least one request is in flight.

values.name: Completed
values.doc: Every request finished successfully.

values.name: Failed
values.doc: Finished with at least one asset that failed to resolve.

values.name: Cancelled
values.doc: Abandoned before completion.

types.summary: Outcome of a Gantry operation that can fail in more than one interesting way.

values.name: Success
values.doc: The operation completed.

values.name: Pending
values.doc: Accepted and still running; a completion delegate will fire later.

values.name: InvalidArgument
values.doc: Arguments were wrong. A programming error, not a runtime condition.

values.name: NotFound
values.doc: The thing being addressed does not exist, or its handle is stale.

values.name: NotReady
values.doc: The subsystem is not initialised, or is shutting down.

values.name: Failed
values.doc: Ran, but the result is not usable. Check the log.

values.name: Cancelled
values.doc: Abandoned before completion at the caller's request.

types.summary: Tags GantryCore declares natively.

members.name: InitState_Spawned
members.summary: Component bring-up stages, consumed by the engine's UGameFrameworkComponentManager.
members.description:
Unprefixed, unlike every other tag Gantry declares. These four strings are the vocabulary the engine's modular gameplay samples established, and any third-party component written against that convention expects them by name. Relocating them under Gantry.* would fork the vocabulary and quietly break every component that did not know to follow.

They are declared here so a project does not have to redeclare them. Gantry never advances an actor through the chain itself; driving the sequence is the game's job.

The sequence exists because actor initialisation cannot be ordered in advance: a pawn spawns, its player state replicates whenever the network delivers it, and its data assets finish loading at a third unrelated moment. Rather than guessing an order, each component advances as far as its own prerequisites allow and re-evaluates whenever anything else moves.

properties.name: DefaultExperience
properties.summary: Experience auto-activated when a world begins play and nothing else has set one.
properties.description:
Optional.

Lives here rather than in project settings because it is a content decision: the root declares its tree, so it declares its starting leaf too. Any experience reachable from this base qualifies — a direct child or a deeper descendant; validation rejects anything the tree cannot reach, because an unreachable default is a boot into a guaranteed failure.

types.summary: A named composite of content, activated in stages.

properties.name: ExperienceTag
properties.summary: Identifies this experience, so game code can react without a hard asset reference.

properties.name: ExperienceGuid
properties.summary: Machine identity: assigned once at asset creation, regenerated on duplication, never edited.
properties.description: Three identities, three jobs. The asset *path* is where it lives and breaks on a move. The *tag* is the human identity — designer-authored, used by code and UI, and renameable when a taxonomy changes. The *guid* survives both, which is what save games, server verification, and mod databases need: a name for the content that no refactor can invalidate.

properties.name: DisplayNameOverride
properties.summary: Optional display name.
properties.description: Empty means "use the asset name".

properties.name: Description
properties.summary: One or two lines for a store or selection screen.
properties.description: Shown even while this content is absent.

properties.name: Metadata
properties.summary: Provenance and compatibility for this experience as a shipped unit.

properties.name: Stages
properties.summary: Stages run in order during activation, and unwound in reverse on deactivation.
properties.description: Instanced, so each experience configures its own.

properties.name: Payload
properties.summary: Free-form payload for the game.
properties.description: Gantry never reads this. It exists so a project can attach its own data object without subclassing, which is often enough and keeps the asset type count down.

properties.name: Children
properties.summary: Experiences that belong under this one.
properties.description:
Owner side of the tree.

Just the assets — everything about a child (tag, name, description, metadata) is authored on the child itself, which is the only place it makes sense to live. Each child may be listed by exactly one parent; a duplicate listing is a validation error.

Soft on purpose: a listed child's content may not be mounted, and the listing must survive that. ChildSnapshots below is what keeps an absent child describable.

properties.name: ChildSnapshots
properties.summary: Cook-time copies of each child's display data, for when the child itself is absent.
properties.description: Machine-written by RebuildChildSnapshots during cook, and deliberately absent from the details panel: there is no correct human interaction with a machine-maintained cache, so it offers none. Inspect it through the tree's availability queries, or a debugger.

properties.name: OptionalDependencies
properties.summary: Experiences this one wants but does not need.
properties.description:
Wanter side; never gates activation.

A present optional dependency joins the activation chain and is ordered before this experience. An absent one is skipped, and it is this experience's responsibility to cope — query UGantryExperienceSubsystem::IsExperienceActive and branch.

properties.name: AttachTo
properties.summary: Required parent(s), declared by side-loaded content that no shipped asset can list.
properties.description: Shipped content leaves this empty and gets its parent from whoever lists it. Multiple entries are legal for side-loaded content only — the compatibility-patch pattern, "requires A and B" — and every named parent must resolve or this experience is an orphan.

properties.name: bIsTreeRoot
properties.summary: True on the tree root, which cannot have dependencies — an optional want from the root points at its own descendant (a cycle by construction) or at side-loaded content (nonsense), and an attachment contradicts being the root.
properties.description: Set by UGantryBaseExperienceDefinition's constructor; exists so the editor hides those fields instead of offering wrong answers.

types.summary: Loads and activates game feature plugins.

properties.name: GameFeaturePluginNames
properties.summary: Plugin names, not URLs.
properties.description: Gantry resolves each to a URL at activation time.

properties.name: bDeactivateOnEnd
properties.summary: Release this stage's plugin references when the experience ends.
properties.description: Release, not deactivate: a plugin another experience still holds stays up. Turning this off leaks references for the lifetime of the process and is only ever right for a plugin that must outlive every experience.

properties.name: ActivatedPluginURLs
properties.summary: Plugins this stage activated, recorded on every engine.
properties.description:
On 5.6 / 5.7 these are the references this stage holds in Gantry's process-wide counts, and teardown releases exactly these.

On 5.8+ they back the handle. FGameFeatureStateHandle is gated behind GameFeatureStateHandle.Enabled, which the engine describes as "a quick way for now to disable and fallback to how things are now". If that CVar is off, InitAndRegister leaves the handle invalid and releasing it would silently free nothing, leaking every plugin an experience ever activated. So teardown falls back to direct deactivation of these URLs, unreference counted, which is the behaviour the CVar asked for.

functions.name: SetExperienceByTag
functions.summary: Activates an experience by identity, replacing any current one.
functions.description: The tag is resolved through the crawled tree: the leaf's required chain plus its present optional dependencies, ordered shallow to deep. An experience the tree does not know cannot activate — being listed (or being side-loaded content whose attachment resolves) is what makes activation possible. Asynchronous; listen on OnExperienceReady.
